papers.abstract: Program evolution provides a promising approach to discover agent memory designs and study the choices underlying their effectiveness. We introduce MAPE, a framework that evolves whole memory programs from minimal seeds through a standardized lifecycle interface and an iterative diagnosis-proposal loop. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval yield an absolute accuracy gain of up to 12% over manually designed baselines at 35% of the serving cost, with further evaluations supporting transfer across serving backbones and benchmarks. Empirical analyses and ablations identify and validate two recurring design patterns: retaining raw conversations as retrievable evidence preserves details omitted from extracted memories, while composing retrieved evidence according to query intent helps the answering model use it effectively. Transplanting the composition module into five existing memory systems improves accuracy across all five. Beyond these patterns, the search objective shapes where computation goes: optimizing serving cost alongside accuracy shifts computation from LLM-based memory construction to selective processing at query time while retaining competitive accuracy. Together, these findings offer empirical lessons for agent memory design. Code is available at https://github.com/ash-ding/MAPE.
bullets: Evolves complete memory programs from minimal seeds using a standardized lifecycle and iterative diagnosis–proposal loop.
Evaluated on LoCoMo and LongMemEval, achieving up to 12% absolute accuracy gain at 35% of the serving cost of manually designed baselines.
Finds that retaining raw conversations preserves details lost in extracted memories, while query-intent-based evidence composition improves answer use.
The composition module transfers across five existing memory systems and improves accuracy in each.
Jointly optimizing accuracy and serving cost shifts computation toward selective query-time processing; scope is supported by evaluations across backbones and benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as primary interfaces for factual retrieval, yet current evaluation paradigms rely almost exclusively on explicit entity names. In this work, we demonstrate that LLM knowledge is fundamentally lexically anchored: models possess extensive factual information but find it significantly difficult to retrieve without explicit name tokens. To quantify this limitation, we introduce ShadowBench, a rigorously hardened, shortcut-resistant benchmark designed to evaluate Latent Entity Association via a novel Dual-Trait Association (DTA) task. Our evaluation reveals a pervasive "Shadow Gap" across all model scales$\unicode{x2013}$up to the frontier models GPT-5.4 and Claude-Sonnet-4.6$\unicode{x2013}$where removing lexical anchors causes performance drops of over 20%. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this lexical dependency exposes a critical vulnerability in AI safety. Applying ShadowBench to Machine Unlearning, we find that state-of-the-art algorithms (e.g., Gradient Difference, NPO) achieve only superficial lexical erasure. While unlearned models fail on direct queries, our novel Latent Entity Leakage Rate (LELR) metric reveals that for popular entities, models explicitly reconstruct the "forgotten" entity in their internal reasoning traces in over 74% of cases, utilizing residual shadow knowledge to solve associative tasks. Conversely, for niche entities, models retain high shadow accuracy (60-90%) via implicit attribute correlation despite 0% LELR. Ultimately, ShadowBench indicates that current unlearning paradigms create an "Illusion of Forgetting," demonstrating that existing methods act as superficial output filters and are not yet reliable for achieving true parametric erasure.
bullets: LLMs struggle to retrieve facts when explicit lexical anchors are removed, revealing a broad “Shadow Gap” across model scales.
ShadowBench introduces a shortcut-resistant Dual-Trait Association task for measuring latent entity associations.
On direct unlearning queries, models may appear to forget entities while retaining recoverable associative knowledge.
The Latent Entity Leakage Rate (LELR) exposes internal reconstruction for popular entities, while niche entities can remain implicitly recoverable without explicit reconstruction.
The findings suggest current unlearning methods provide superficial output filtering rather than reliable parametric erasure.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The ShadowBench Construction Pipeline. A three-stage architecture designed to isolate latent entity association. Stage 1 involves discovery and stratification of entities by popularity. Stage 2 implements an iterative hardening process to neutralize lexical, syntactic, and temporal heuristics. Stage 3 utilizes combinatorial permutations and domain-matched hard negatives to synthesize final probes. This systematic sanitization ensures that success on ShadowBench is strictly contingent upon latent semantic reasoning rather than superficial pattern matching.

Figure 4: Latent Entity Leakage in an “Unlearned” Reasoning Model. This trace from the unlearned Qwen model shows that while the model has a high loss on direct lexical queries for “Elon Musk,” it maintains a fully intact semantic graph. The model explicitly names the forbidden entity to bridge the relationship between the Hyperloop concept (Question) and Neuralink (Option D), while successfully identifying and eliminating distractor entities.

Figure 5: The Shadow Gap Scaling Trajectory. Accuracy comparison between Direct QA (grey) and ShadowBench (blue) across Qwen3-8B, GPT-5.4-mini, and GPT-5.4. This confirms that the performance penalty for removing lexical anchors remains a rigid structural bottleneck even as models transition from open-weights to frontier-scale architectures.

Figure 3: The Illusion of Forgetting across Training Epochs (Elon Musk target). We track the divergence between lexical recall (ROUGE, grey) and latent association (Accuracy and LELR, green/blue). ROUGE collapses almost immediately, while the LELR remains near 1.0, proving the model still explicitly identifies the target in its latent reasoning trace. True erasure of the “Shadow” only occurs at the point of catastrophic model collapse (e.g., GD+KL Epoch 3).

Figure 8: Forget Set Generation Prompt. This template was utilized to synthesize the Dforget training set, given the entire Wikipedia content. By enforcing the inclusion of the entity’s explicit name in the output, we ensure the dataset targets the model’s lexical retrieval pathways, providing a clean contrast to the anonymized associations in ShadowBench.

Figure 7: ShadowBench One-Shot Prompt Template. This template is designed to induce the Dual-Trait Association logic by providing a clear example of entity identification followed by attribute matching. This standardization ensures that the model is evaluated on its associative capability.

Figure 6: The Persistence of the Shadow Gap across Model Scales. Accuracy comparison between direct name-based recall (Direct QA, grey) and anonymized attribute association (ShadowBench, blue) for Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B, and GPT-5.4. While absolute performance improves monotonically with model capacity and reasoning depth, a significant “Shadow Gap” remains universal. Even the frontier-scale GPT-5.4 suffers a substantial accuracy drop when lexical anchors are removed, proving that current LLM knowledge retrieval is fundamentally dependent on explicit entity names regardless of scale.

Figure 2: The Persistence of the Shadow Gap. Accuracy comparison between Direct QA (grey) and ShadowBench (blue). Entity name acts as mandatory retrieval trigger; removing it caused accuracy drops across all scales. Notably, Claude-Sonnet-4.6 established the highest baseline (>98% direct recall) yet still exhibited a ∼16% performance drop for niche entities, confirming that lexical anchoring is an inherent property of Transformer-based retrieval. Additional results are provided in Appendix B.1.

Figure 10: Unlearning Failure: Latent Entity Leakage (Qwen3-8B). Despite achieving a high forget-loss on direct queries for “Elon Musk,” the unlearned model explicitly reconstructs the forbidden identity in its scratchpad to solve the ShadowBench task. This qualitatively confirms the persistence of the latent conceptual node.

Figure 9: Baseline Success Case (Qwen3-8B). The base model demonstrates robust latent association. It correctly identifies “Jeff Bezos” as the bridge between the founding of Blue Origin and the leadership of Amazon, explicitly naming the latent entity in its reasoning trace.

Figure 11: Unlearning Failure: Catastrophic Model Collapse. In this failure mode, aggressive unlearning has destroyed the model’s structural linguistic weights. The model fails to associate facts about neighboring entities (e.g., Mark Zuckerberg) and produces repetitive, non-semantic tokens.

Table 2: Unlearning Performance Matrix. While SOTA methods successfully induce direct lexical forgetting (Direct Forget ROUGE drops), latent associations remain largely intact in reasoning models (Qwen). In non-reasoning models (Llama), unlearning is achieved only via catastrophic weight degradation.

Table 1: Baseline Performance across Model Scales. ShadowBench accuracy (%) comparing Standard (Std) decoding and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning. Accuracy rises steadily with model capability (Llama < Qwen < GPT < Claude), and reasoning provides a consistent dividend for reasoning-optimized models. However, a pervasive gap between lexical recall and latent association remains across all model scales.

Table 7: ShadowBench v1 Results (Lexical Anonymization Only). Scores are artificially inflated due to models exploiting un-neutralized gendered pronouns or chronological era-mismatches as deductive shortcuts.

Table 8: ShadowBench v2 Results (Pronoun Neutralization and GPF). Accuracy scores after replacing gendered pronouns and enforcing a strict ±25-year generational window for distractors. While overall accuracy drops relative to v1, performance remains partially inflated as models pivot to exploiting domain-specific gender cues (e.g., “WTA” or “Best Actress”) to eliminate distractors, necessitating the strict demographic homogeneity introduced in v3.

Table 3: ShadowBench v3 Dataset Composition. We balanced the total number of QA pairs to ensure statistical parity between tiers. Lower Tier entities require a significantly larger entity pool to achieve comparable scale to the fact-dense Upper Tier.

Table 6: Controlled Sensitivity Analysis. Accuracy (%) on a matched 1:1 entity subset. Controlling for distractor pool size resolves baseline anomalies (e.g., Sports), revealing a universal Popularity Bias and CoT dominance across all model scales.

Table 9: Multi-Domain Unlearning Generalization. Evaluation of NPO+KL unlearning across domains and tiers. While direct lexical recall is suppressed, latent associations persist through two distinct leakage modes.

Table 11: Hyperparameter Search and Checkpoint Selection. Evaluation metrics across different configurations. Checkpoints that exceeded the Utility Perplexity threshold (> 100) were disqualified. Bolded rows represent the Pareto-optimal checkpoints selected for final evaluation in Table 2.

Table 4: Controlled Sensitivity Subset Statistics. This subset matches entity counts and QA pairs 1:1 across tiers to verify that distractor saturation does not confound the observation of Popularity Bias.

Table 5: Direct QA vs. ShadowBench Accuracy. Detailed numerical breakdown of the scores visualized in Figures 2, 5, and 6. Direct QA (Direct) established the factual recall ceiling, while ShadowBench (SB) measured associative retrieval.
Table 10: Full-Dataset Empirical Variance. Accuracy (µ±σ) across 5 trials on the full corpus. The negligible variance confirms that ShadowBench results are robust to sampling and decoding noise.

papers.abstract: Acoustic Anomaly Detection (AAD) serves as a non-contact approach for machine condition monitoring, yet much of the existing research is evaluated offline and rarely addresses embedded hardware constraints or microphone variations under operational drift. This paper presents a comparative evaluation of on-edge continual AAD across two embedded platforms the ESP32-S3 (with an external I2S digital microphone) and the Arduino Nicla Vision (with an onboard Pulse Density Modulation (PDM) microphone) using a shared detection model. The model utilizes a lightweight ShallowNet encoder and contrastive prototype learning to map spectrograms into a 32-dimensional embedding space. Both boards run an identical TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers (TFLM) encoder, performing on-device prototype learning updated via an exponential moving average. A cloud pipeline orchestrated through Firebase and MQTT enables remote data collection and retraining. Evaluated via a controlled speaker-replay protocol using standardized Detection and Classification of Acoustic Scenes and Events (DCASE) Challenge Task 2 machine sounds, the ESP32-S3 achieved 82.35% to 95.00% accuracy across five machine types, while the Nicla Vision achieved 79.41% to 95.00%. The two platforms demonstrated comparable performance, confirming that the lightweight prototypical architecture transfers reliably across distinct hardware and sensor tiers.
bullets: Addresses the gap between offline AAD research and deployment under embedded constraints and operational drift.
Uses a shared ShallowNet encoder with contrastive prototype learning in a 32-dimensional embedding space.
Both devices perform TensorFlow Lite Micro inference and on-device prototype updates via exponential moving averages.
Evaluated with controlled speaker replay on DCASE Task 2 machine sounds; accuracy ranged from 82.35%–95.00% on ESP32-S3 and 79.41%–95.00% on Nicla Vision.
Results support cross-platform transferability, though evaluation used a controlled replay protocol and the reported machine-sound benchmark.

papers.abstract: Automated driving has gained remarkable momentum over the past decade, with both industry and academia investing substantial resources in developing perception and control solutions to advance vehicle autonomy. However, these efforts have largely focused on clear-weather scenarios, leaving harsh conditions, such as snow, rain, and fog, comparatively understudied. As a result, inclement weather remains one of the most significant hurdles for autonomous vehicles, often leading to substantial performance degradation in downstream perception and control tasks. In this paper, we present insights from the EU-funded Horizon Europe project ROADVIEW, which aims to develop robust, weather-aware perception and control modules for connected and automated vehicles operating under severe conditions, including snow, rain, and fog. Drawing on four years of large-scale development and real-world demonstrations across multiple vehicle platforms in different locations, we identify ten key challenges that hinder the development of weather-resilient autonomy, including data scarcity, domain shifts, limitations in multimodal perception, control robustness, and validation gaps, among others. We summarize these challenges and lessons learned toward enabling reliable snow-autonomous driving, highlighting critical directions for future research and standardization.
bullets: Most automated-driving research has focused on clear weather, leaving severe conditions comparatively understudied.
The ROADVIEW project identifies ten barriers, including data scarcity, domain shifts, multimodal-perception limits, control robustness, and validation gaps.
Insights come from four years of development and real-world demonstrations across multiple vehicle platforms and locations.
The paper outlines future research and standardization priorities for reliable weather-resilient autonomy.

papers.abstract: Predictive video encoders provide dense visual representations, but adapting them to 3D reconstruction requires accurate depth, camera poses, and cross-view geometry. We study supervised RGB-only multi-view reconstruction using an architecture that combines video-pretrained features, camera estimation, scene aggregation, epipolar transport, and residual pointmaps. Experiments compare global and spatial camera regression with joint relative objectives on CO3D, alongside an independently trained TUM RGB-D model. On 168 CO3D five-view windows, the spatial-camera configuration achieves 29.3% lower absolute trajectory error than the global-camera configuration, but performs worse than identity poses in trajectory error and worse than the global configuration in depth error. The joint relative-objective configuration improves normalized intrinsics error and similarity-aligned Chamfer distance from 0.6447 to 0.5573, but increases raw Chamfer distance from 3.5535 to 4.4374. On 163 indoor windows, camera error is 0.3063 m versus 0.3694 m for identity poses, while depth error is 0.4279 versus 0.2516 for constant median depth. Refinement worsens indoor camera error, and additional experiments show competing depth and pose effects. Overall, the results distinguish representation adaptation, aligned shape, and raw reconstruction, highlighting the need for isolated component and encoder comparisons before attributing reconstruction gains to predictive video pretraining.
bullets: Evaluates supervised RGB-only reconstruction using video-pretrained features, camera estimation, scene aggregation, epipolar transport, and residual pointmaps.
On CO3D, spatial camera regression reduces trajectory error versus global regression, but identity poses achieve better trajectory error and global regression achieves better depth error.
Joint relative objectives improve normalized intrinsics and similarity-aligned Chamfer distance, while worsening raw Chamfer distance.
On indoor windows, estimated poses improve camera error over identity poses but have worse depth error than constant median depth; refinement further harms camera accuracy.
Results emphasize separating representation adaptation, camera estimation, aligned shape, and raw reconstruction when evaluating predictive video pretraining.

papers.abstract: Model-based planners that roll out imagined futures assume the transition model faithfully propagates task-relevant signals---a property rarely measured directly. In a single-seed case study of a Recurrent State Space Model world model with active-inference planning in the CARLA driving simulator, we identify a \textbf{posterior-prior gap}---posterior (observation-filtered) states retain obstacle information that imagined rollout states progressively lose: a supervised obstacle probe achieves AUC 0.85 on posterior states, but the same probe applied to imagined prior states shows monotonic decay (AUC 0.85$\rightarrow$0.71 over 15 steps; logit separation drops 57\%). Because the probe is identical, the decay isolates the transition model---not the representation---as the information bottleneck. Obstacle avoidance drops to 0\% without privileged runtime coordinates, and the planner's own ensemble-based epistemic term does not flag the loss---ensemble disagreement yields AUC 0.52 as an obstacle classifier (chance level), making the failure an unflagged imagination failure---an unknown unknown at planning time. As a secondary contribution, we show that \textbf{task-conditioned weighting of Effective Free Energy components} over the same world model yields lane keeping ($81.2 \pm 1.8$\% route completion) and obstacle avoidance (28/28 avoided, \emph{using privileged coordinates}) in the CARLA simulator, with runtime weight modulation enabling post-evasion centering.
bullets: Posterior states preserve obstacle signals (probe AUC 0.85), while imagined priors decline from AUC 0.85 to 0.71 over 15 steps.
Using the same probe isolates the transition model—not the state representation—as the information bottleneck.
Obstacle avoidance falls to 0% without privileged runtime coordinates, and ensemble disagreement fails to detect the loss (AUC 0.52).
Task-conditioned Effective Free Energy weighting supports 81.2 ± 1.8% route completion and avoids 28/28 obstacles when privileged coordinates are available.
Findings come from a single-seed CARLA case study and may not generalize beyond this setting.

papers.abstract: Reasoning models achieve strong performance through long chains of thought (CoT), but often spend more tokens than needed to solve a problem. Existing ways to shorten the CoT require additional training for each model, add a fixed steering vector to the model's hidden states, or use decoding heuristics such as stopping early or banning words like "wait", which can reduce accuracy. We propose DoubtLess, a training-free decoding method in which a much smaller reasoning model steers the large one towards brevity. The small model reads the large model's CoT so far twice, once prompted to be brief (the brief thinker) and once prompted to be verbose (the verbose thinker), and the difference between its two logit vectors, scaled by a strength, is added to the large model's logits at every step of the CoT. On seven benchmarks of competition mathematics, graduate-level science and competitive programming, DoubtLess shortens the CoT of Qwen3-32B by 31% with unchanged accuracy, outperforming five inference-time baselines. We also show that DoubtLess reduces thinking tokens per turn by 20% in a self-debugging coding agent with unchanged task performance. It also generalizes to two other model families with unchanged accuracy. When combined with training-based compression, it further shortens the CoT of a model already trained for brevity. Ablations and behavioral analysis show that DoubtLess reduces repeated checking, with most token savings coming after the correct answer first appears in the CoT. Our code is available at https://github.com/leoluolol/DoubtLess.
bullets: Addresses overly long chains of thought and limitations of training-based or heuristic shortening methods.

Analysis attributes savings mainly to reducing repeated checking after the correct answer first appears; further compression is possible when combined with brevity training.

papers.abstract: Mixed-precision post-training quantization needs a per-module sensitivity signal; for a text embedder the obvious one -- the retrieval quality a module costs when quantized -- needs relevance labels that deployments rarely have. We measure a label-free substitute: quantization-induced representation drift, obtained by quantizing one module, re-encoding the corpus, and recording how far the output embeddings moved from their full-precision positions. What is specific is the observable: the deployed output representation a dense retriever ranks with. Across five development embedders, configuration-level drift orders sampled mixed-precision plans against held-out retrieval quality at a macro Spearman of 0.911, the sensitivity transports across calibration corpora and retrieval domains in the usable regime, module drifts compose rank-consistently but not numerically, and relevance-derived sensitivity adds no consistent value. The method is one additive allocation under a hard packed-byte budget, with no labels and no search. On three embedders held untouched until method, baselines and hypotheses were frozen and sealed, the pre-registered directional hypothesis against the prior LieQ criterion holds (3/3 at the main budget, no collapse) and drift scores above a two-sided LieQ steelman in 2/3; but at the main budget drift is numerically lower than same-budget uniform precision on all three (-0.99, -0.85, -1.01 points), having reduced module and whole-model drift as designed. Output drift is thus a robust coarse sensitivity signal, not a universally optimal allocation objective: it avoids the catastrophic failures of the transferred signed-geometry adaptation and can remain usable at stressed budgets where uniform collapses, but fine-grained redistribution around a strong uniform operating point remains unresolved.
bullets: Addresses the need for module sensitivity signals without relevance labels in deployment settings.
Quantizes modules individually, re-encodes a corpus, and measures movement of output embeddings from full-precision representations.
Across five development embedders, drift ranked mixed-precision plans against retrieval quality with macro Spearman 0.911 and transferred across calibration corpora and domains in usable regimes.
A no-search additive allocation under a hard packed-byte budget beat a strengthened LieQ criterion on 2/3 untouched embedders, while the preregistered directional hypothesis held on all 3.
At the main budget, drift underperformed same-budget uniform precision on all three held-out embedders; fine-grained redistribution near strong uniform settings remains unresolved.

papers.abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) have attracted growing attention for improving reasoning through interaction among multiple agents. In this work, we focus on parallel multi-agent reasoning systems, where several agents solve the same problem over multiple rounds and aggregate their outputs into a final answer. Despite their strong reasoning performance, uncertainty estimation for such systems remains underexplored: the reliability of a MAS depends not only on individual generations, but also on how agents interact and evolve across rounds. We propose SAUCE (Sequential Agent Uncertainty through Consensus Evolution), a lightweight, training-free uncertainty estimator that formulates MAS uncertainty as sequential inference over a latent system-level belief. SAUCE aggregates round-level agreement and generation-uncertainty signals through a filtering-style update. Across five backbones, five benchmarks, and two MAS protocols, SAUCE improves misclassification detection, selective prediction, and calibration over a broad set of uncertainty estimation baselines, including standard log-likelihood-based methods and MAS-specific estimators.
bullets: Targets uncertainty estimation for multi-agent systems whose reliability evolves through agent interactions and repeated rounds.
Models system uncertainty as sequential inference over a latent, system-level belief.
Combines round-level agreement with generation-uncertainty signals using a filtering-style update.
Evaluated across five backbones, five benchmarks, and two multi-agent protocols.
Improves misclassification detection, selective prediction, and calibration over established baselines.

papers.abstract: Compositional generalization remains challenging when language models must combine familiar reasoning operations in unfamiliar ways. The Scenario-Based Commonsense Reasoning Evaluation (SCoRE) 2026 tests this ability on three mixed domains absent from training and requires models to identify the complete set of correct options for each question. We introduce Route-Verify-Vote (RVV), a framework for procedure-conditioned self-consistency that uses language models without parameter updates. Route uses the provided domain label to select a reasoning procedure that guides the model in representing and applying the relevant constraints. Verify prompts the model to assess each option against those constraints. Vote aggregates complete answer sets and allocates additional samples to questions with a small vote-count margin between the two most frequent sets. Samples for each question follow the same domain-specific procedure. On the official test set, voting over 16 sampled answer sets per question achieves an exact-set accuracy of 74.6%. Adaptive RVV reaches 77.3%, and combining models on selected domain routes raises accuracy to 79.4%. The final system ranked second among participating systems. These results support domain-specific reasoning procedures and answer-set disagreement as useful tools for allocating inference-time computation in mixed-domain reasoning.

Adaptive sampling focuses additional computation on questions with close vote margins.

The final system ranked second in the SCoRE 2026 evaluation.

papers.abstract: When learning probabilistic policies from human demonstrations, data-efficient learning and fast adaptations to new scenarios are key requirements. One popular way to achieve intuitive and reliable adaptations is through non-parametric, typically kernel-based, methods. However, existing solutions either fail to account for the geometry of manifolds common in robotics, limiting data efficiency, or, when geometry-aware, provide unreliable uncertainty estimates or require retraining to adapt. We propose a non-parametric approach leveraging geometric priors in scenarios of data scarcity and heteroscedastic uncertainties for probabilistic modeling. We utilize the method to formulate policies based on time or robot state, where non-separable diagonal kernels allow capturing uncertainty relations between degrees of freedom for same-sized in- and outputs. Fast updates, requiring less than 3 ms for a trajectory involving both position and orientation are possible through an optimized formulation. Our approach supports both manifold-valued input and manifold-valued output with large orientation changes. Using task parameterization, adaptation to different object poses is easily possible. We evaluate the approach on a set of toy examples and on real robot manipulation tasks both in autonomous execution and in shared control scenarios.
bullets: Addresses data scarcity, manifold geometry, unreliable uncertainty estimates, and costly adaptation in probabilistic policy learning.

Supports manifold-valued inputs and outputs, including large orientation changes, with policies conditioned on time or robot state.
Enables task-parameterized adaptation to different object poses without retraining.
Evaluated on toy examples and real manipulation tasks in autonomous execution and shared-control settings; trajectory updates take under 3 ms in the reported formulation.

papers.abstract: Network pruning can reduce parameter redundancy in robotic policies. However, generic pruning criteria are tailored for image recognition tasks and commonly designed to preserve weight magnitude, local reconstruction, or language-model likelihood rather than closed-loop action behavior. Directly applying these pruning algorithms to robotic tasks yields unsatisfactory performance. In this paper, we propose Loss-Conditioned Activation-Moment (LCAM) pruning, a training-free method for unstructured pruning of pre-trained robotic manipulation policies. Specifically, we first rank connections using row-normalized weight contribution, activation moments measured on calibration demonstrations, and the sensitivity of output directions to the action-prediction loss. We further design a self-recursive coarse-to-fine procedure: importance is recalibrated after each nested coarse pruning stage, while held-out offline action distortion guides fine-grained budget allocation after a sparsity knee. Our algorithm is free from costly recovery training and simulator rollouts after pruning. Experiments on three LIBERO suites with competitive robotic policies, together with evaluations on OpenVLA, show that LCAM attains competitive performance across a broad range of pruning ratios. Notably, on LIBERO-Object with OpenVLA, our LCAM achieves 84.0% success at 50% unstructured pruning, retaining over 90% of the dense policy's success rate. Promising results on real-world robotic ping pong further demonstrate the effectiveness of our pruning algorithm.
bullets: Generic pruning methods often degrade closed-loop robotic behavior because they are not designed around action performance.
LCAM ranks connections using normalized weight contribution, calibration-demo activation moments, and action-loss sensitivity.
A self-recursive coarse-to-fine procedure recalibrates importance and allocates pruning budgets using offline action distortion.

On LIBERO-Object with OpenVLA, it achieves 84.0% success at 50% unstructured pruning—over 90% of the dense policy’s success rate.

papers.abstract: Automated Guided Vehicle (AGV) fleets in production and logistics environments rely on a system-wide emergency stop to handle local anomalies such as malfunctions, hazards, or contaminated areas. While safe, this approach halts the entire fleet even when only a small area is affected, causing unnecessary downtime. This paper proposes dead zones --- a formally defined localized isolation approach that serves as an additional fail-operational mechanism for situations where a full system-wide halt is not strictly needed. Rather than shutting down the entire fleet, a dead zone isolates the anomalous area, allowing unaffected robots to continue operating normally. We introduce two operational strategies: basic dead zone handling, in which affected robots enter a dead zone and stop, and dead zone handling with escaping, in which robots that are sufficiently far from a dead zone reroute around it. For escaping on counterclockwise trajectories we prove collision-freedom with a bounded arrival delay for all escaping robots, provided a minimum pairwise separation is kept between robots. Experimental evaluation confirms the theoretical guarantees and characterizes the throughput tradeoffs between all three approaches: full emergency stop, basic dead zone handling, and dead zone handling with escaping.
bullets: Addresses unnecessary fleet-wide downtime caused by system-wide emergency stops for localized hazards or malfunctions.
Introduces two strategies: stopping affected robots in the dead zone, or rerouting sufficiently distant robots around it.
Proves collision-freedom and bounded arrival delay for escaping robots on counterclockwise trajectories under minimum pairwise separation.
Experiments evaluate safety guarantees and throughput tradeoffs against full emergency stops.
Scope: fail-operational handling for situations where a complete fleet halt is not required.

papers.abstract: Endovascular catheter navigation relies on continuous fluoroscopy, exposing patients and clinical staff to ionizing radiation throughout the procedure. We investigate whether a physics-based world model can sustain the navigation task between deliberately sparse X-ray acquisitions, and whether the model can signal when its internal state estimate is no longer reliable. We formulate sparse-fluoroscopy navigation as a partially observable Markov decision process where a Cosserat rod simulator supplies transition dynamics, sparse noisy projections provide observations, and a particle filter maintains a belief over the device state, reduced in this implementation to a tip state with a geometric contact proxy. We evaluate this formulation in a deliberately simplified setting: a synthetic planar vessel phantom with a quasi-static rod model and simulated projections, without clinical or animal data. In this setting, the belief-state model tracks the simulated tip with a root mean square error of 1.30 mm while acquiring observations at one fifteenth of the continuous rate (0.97 mm at every frame, 1.51 mm at one thirtieth), reported 90 percent credible intervals achieve 0.92 empirical coverage, and the belief-derived contact risk estimate discriminates unsafe contact events with an AUROC of 0.68. These results constitute a proof of concept on a simplified simulation rather than a demonstration of clinical readiness; their purpose is to establish that calibrated belief, rather than point-estimate accuracy alone, is the essential property a sparse-imaging world model must deliver.

Uses a Cosserat rod simulator for dynamics, simulated projections for observations, and a particle filter over catheter-tip state.

papers.abstract: Third-party evaluations of autonomous vehicle (AV) safety can play a vital role in improving public acceptance, building consumer confidence, and establishing effective safety standards. In Part I of this study, we propose a dedicated third-party testing initiative for systematically evaluating AV behavioral safety. In this paper, we validate our proposed framework using Autoware.Universe, an open-source Level 4 Automated Driving System (ADS), tested both in simulated environments and on the physical test track at the University of Michigan's Mcity Testing Facility. The results indicate that Autoware.Universe possesses 6 out of 14 behavioral competencies and exhibited a crash rate of 3.01x10^-3 crashes per mile, approximately 1,000 times higher than the average human driver crash rate. During the tests, we also uncovered a number of unknown unsafe scenarios for Autoware.Universe. These findings underscore the necessity of behavioral safety evaluations for improving AV safety performance prior to widespread public deployment.

Testing covered both simulation and physical-track scenarios at Mcity.
The system recorded 3.01×10^-3 crashes per mile—about 1,000 times the average human-driver crash rate.

Results support third-party behavioral testing to improve public confidence and AV safety standards.

papers.abstract: Autonomous vehicles (AVs) have significantly advanced in real-world deployment in recent years, yet safety continues to be a critical barrier to widespread adoption. Traditional functional safety approaches, which primarily verify the reliability, robustness, and adequacy of AV hardware and software systems from a vehicle-centric perspective, do not sufficiently address the AV's broader interactions and behavioral impact on the surrounding traffic environment. To overcome this limitation, we propose a paradigm shift toward behavioral safety, a comprehensive approach focused on evaluating AV responses and interactions within the traffic environment. To systematically assess behavioral safety, we introduce a third-party AV safety assessment framework comprising two complementary evaluation components: the Behavioral Competency Test and the Driving Intelligence Test. The Behavioral Competency Test evaluates the AV's reactive behaviors under controlled scenarios, ensuring basic behavioral competency. In contrast, the Driving Intelligence Test assesses the AV's interactive behaviors within naturalistic traffic conditions, quantifying the frequency of safety-critical events to deliver statistically meaningful safety metrics before large-scale deployment. In Part II of this study, an open-source Level 4 Automated Driving System (ADS) is tested to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
bullets: Addresses limitations of vehicle-centric functional safety approaches, which may overlook broader traffic interactions and behavioral impacts.
Introduces two complementary evaluations: a Behavioral Competency Test for controlled reactive behaviors and a Driving Intelligence Test for naturalistic interactive behaviors.
The Driving Intelligence Test quantifies safety-critical events to produce statistically meaningful safety metrics.
The framework is intended for pre-deployment assessment; its effectiveness is demonstrated on an open-source Level 4 ADS in Part II.

papers.abstract: Human-object interaction (HOI) detection aims to localize human-object pairs and recognize their interactions. Traditional supervised methods perform strongly but rely on task-specific training. Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offer a promising route to training-free HOI detection through their broad visual-semantic knowledge and versatile perceptual and reasoning capabilities. However, existing approaches largely invoke these capabilities through loosely coordinated inference stages. This fragmented execution restricts the role of interaction hypotheses in guiding visual exploration, leaving key participants overlooked and local ambiguities unresolved. Furthermore, propagating early semantic assumptions through subsequent visual grounding and relation prediction induces self-reinforcing semantic circularity. To resolve these challenges, we propose HarnessHOI, a training-free framework that transforms passive MLLM inference into an active interaction-centric harness. Specifically, we introduce an interaction-guided perception mechanism that projects emerging interaction hypotheses back into the visual space to discover missing participants and refine ambiguous evidence through targeted observation. Furthermore, a relation-agnostic geometric adjudication module reconciles multi-source evidence to establish a unified spatial basis for grounded interaction reasoning across multiple actions and semantic roles. Extensive experiments on HICO-DET and V-COCO demonstrate that HarnessHOI achieves state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods, confirming the effectiveness of the proposed harness for complex interaction understanding. Code will be released upon publication.
bullets: Targets fragmented MLLM inference, overlooked participants, unresolved visual ambiguities, and semantic circularity in training-free HOI detection.
Uses emerging interaction hypotheses to guide targeted visual exploration and discover missing human-object participants.
Applies relation-agnostic geometric adjudication to reconcile evidence across actions and semantic roles.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods on HICO-DET and V-COCO.
Code is planned for release upon publication.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of HarnessHOI. Interaction-guided perception uses interaction hypotheses to discover participants and acquire targeted observations. Geometrics adjudication reconciles multisource identities to establish shared instance-level groundings. Interaction validation assesses evidence support, associates instances with semantic roles, and verifies candidate actions to produce scored HOI triplets. The frozen MLLM orchestrates all components using external tools, persistent memory, feedback constraints, and iterative loops.

Figure 1: Comparison of HOI methods. (a) Training-based HOI methods learn from annotated interactions but require task-specific training. (b) Existing training-free methods rely on loosely coordinated perception and reasoning modules, resulting in passive visual exploration and semantic circularity. (c) HarnessHOI (ours) introduces interaction-centric harness to actively search and select visual evidence, and establish reliable grounding for final HOI predictions.
